body: At twenty to six Danny’s bed is empty, the quilt turned back square. Out the window, in a gray rain coming down on the old snow, Theo is standing at the bathtub Madonna in the Browns parka with his bare hand on the rim of the tub, and Jack lets the blind go.

By six Nonna has the Pope on the little set at the end of the kitchen counter, up and unhurt on his balcony, blessing the city and the world. Rosie has been awake since a quarter to, sitting on the top stair in her nightgown with Denver the buffalo, because on Christmas morning nobody sets foot in the front room until Nonna is settled, and settling Nonna takes an hour. By ten after seven she is in her chair by the window with the gray cashmere over her knees and her coffee on the sill. Ma puts the Christmas disc in, the same one since Jack was in grade school, and The Band comes on low under the rain, and Rosie comes down the stairs like a fire drill.

There are eight stockings on the mantel this morning. The new one hangs on the end, past NONNA, and the glitter glue on its cuff hasn’t finished drying: THEO. Rosie delivers it to him with both arms. Theo sits on the couch with it across his knees and touches the H, and a little of the H comes off on his finger.
“It’s still wet.”
“I did it Monday night,” Ma says. “Glitter takes a week.”
There’s a tin of her cookies in it, and a tangerine in the toe. Theo keeps the stocking on his lap through everything after.

In Jack’s, under the tangerine, is a page of the phone bill, folded in thirds, the family plan with his line circled in ballpoint, and across the top in Ma’s school-office capitals: UNLIMITED TEXTING. MERRY CHRISTMAS. LOVE, MA. She called them Tuesday. “It was cheaper than you,” Ma says.
Gina sits straight up. “He gets *unlimited*?”
“When you go to California.”

After the stockings, the tree. Rosie delivers, every box, by herself; it’s her job and she’s been training for it all year. Theo’s presents come out of a Neiman Marcus bag one at a time. For Ma, an orange enamel pot from France that weighs more than Rosie, which Ma says is much too much and has the gravy started in before the paper is picked up off the rug. For Nonna, torrone “from the one shop in Beverly Hills a Calabrese would forgive”; Nonna reads the box at arm’s length and forgives it. For Gina, a Flip camera; she’s filming Theo with it before the plastic is off. For Rosie, a stuffed blue crab the size of a hubcap. “*Callinectes sapidus*,” Theo tells her. “The beautiful swimmer.” Rosie says it back to him twice, perfectly, and across the rug Gina looks at Jack. For Danny, by way of Jack, four used paperbacks with the prices still penciled inside the covers. “I *called*,” Theo says. “Softcover only. No staples. They have a list.”

For Frank, last, something flat in tissue. It’s a program: the 1964 championship game, Colts at Browns, Municipal Stadium, December 27th, foxed at the corners and soft with being kept. Frank holds it in both hands a long time.
“Sixty-four,” he says.

Jack’s to Theo is an orange knit hat, the same as Frank’s, and Theo pulls it down over the hair he did something about this morning and doesn’t take it off again. Ma’s is a scarf in brown and orange that she has been knitting in front of the news since Thanksgiving. He puts that on too, and sits there in the Browns’ colors with a stocking in his lap, looking drafted. Nonna has two twenties folded small in the pocket of her housedress, one for each of them. “*Natale.*” Rosie has the markers open in their tin on the rug and is testing the browns.
Ma brings the coffee in from the kitchen on a tray, and it isn’t Folgers. Jack knows it from the first breath: chicory.
“Where’d you get New Orleans coffee?”
“A friend.”
From the chair, over the torrone: “*Della suora.*”

The Priority box from Marisol has been sitting in front of the Nativity since Tuesday. Inside, in white tissue, is a used Vintage paperback of *The Moviegoer*, the spine cracked white in three places and her pencil all down the margins.

body.title: Inside the cover
body.text: For the snow. It’s Carnival in here. —L.

body: Ma reads it over his shoulder. “She *wrote* in it?”
At seven-thirty his pocket buzzes against the couch.

body.text: merry xmas fireman. status of the fixing?
i can tell youre reading this

body: He puts it back in his pocket, and that’s when Rosie comes up with the last thing under the tree. It’s flat and wrapped in the *Vindicator*’s funnies, and Gina sees her pick it up. “Rosie, *no*, that one’s for *later* —” But Rosie has been delivering since seven, and she delivers it.
It’s a DVD box set. *Sweetwater: The Complete Second Season.* On the front, five girls in navy blazers stand on a dock with a lake behind them, and stuck to the shrink-wrap there’s a note.
Gina puts both hands over her face.
“Isn’t that the show with the girls on the lake?” Ma says.

Nonna leans out of her chair and puts her finger on the cover, on the girl in the middle. “*L’attrice!*” She has never seen that face in her life. She’s looking at Gina’s, which is giving everything away.
Theo, in the Browns hat, is very interested in his coffee.
Ma sets the tray down on the coffee table.
“Jack Anthony. Is that the girl?”

choices.key: Christmas morning, with Gina’s DVD in your hands, your mother asked if that was the girl. You told her: that’s her, her name’s Skye.
response: Ma takes the box out of his hands and looks at the cover — the blazer, the dock, the lake — until Gina can’t stand it.
From behind her hands, faintly, Gina says, “She plays the nice one.” She takes her hands down, because it’s over and she knows it. “There’s more,” she tells the room. “It’s on the computer.”

choices.text: “That’s Cassidy. Cassidy’s saving herself for marriage.”
choices.key: Christmas morning, with Gina’s DVD in your hands, your mother asked if that was the girl. You told her that’s Cassidy, and Cassidy’s saving herself for marriage.
response: Frank laughs before he can stop it, one bark, and has to set the 1964 program down very carefully on the arm of his chair so he can wipe his eyes.
Gina is on her feet. “OKAY. Fine. Kitchen. *Everybody.*”

choices.text: “It’s Gina’s. She’s got a crush on the boyfriend.”
choices.key: Christmas morning, with Gina’s DVD in your hands, your mother asked if that was the girl. You told her it was Gina’s crush.
response: Gina looks from her mother to her brother, betrayed down to her socks, and breaks on the spot. “It’s HIS. It’s his GIRLFRIEND.” She’s up off the rug. “Kitchen.”

body: The Dell comes up from the basement at twenty to eight, because Nonna can’t do the stairs and Nonna is not going to miss this. Frank carries the tower, backward, a step at a time, saying what he says on stairs. Theo carries the monitor, in the scarf. Gina carries the keyboard and the extension cord and the authority. Ma clears her list and the sugar bowl off the end of the kitchen table to make room, and the cord goes from the outlet behind the refrigerator across the linoleum to the table, and Frank goes back for Nonna’s chair and sets it in the doorway, and Nonna is helped into it like a bishop into a car.
Jack has pictured this happening a lot of ways since Thanksgiving. None of them had the Dell on the kitchen table next to the butter dish.

His Facebook has been logged in on the Dell since Thanksgiving weekend, his own face in the corner of the page. Gina logs him out with her elbows up, touching nothing she doesn’t have to. “I’m not going *in* yours. I’m not an *animal*.” She logs in as herself.

body.text: She types the name he gave them, spelling it out loud as she goes, S-K-Y-E, for the record.
Ma sits down across the table from him. “Saving herself,” she says, and lets him wonder how long that’s going to keep coming up.
She types with her shoulder turned to him. “Since *some* people lie on Christmas,” she tells the screen, and cracks her knuckles.

body: It takes four minutes.

The fan page first: four thousand and change. “One of them is in *Brazil*.” Gina scrolls the Wall for them like the announcements at Mass: a girl in Tulsa who would die for Cassidy, a girl in Ottawa who already has, a long one in Portuguese with a great many hearts in it. After it, the network’s pictures — the five girls on the dock again, the five girls in a hallway, Skye with her blazer over her shoulder and her chin up. And three of Skye’s own, public, the kind anybody can see: Skye on a red carpet in a dress cut down to there in front; Skye in a bikini on somebody’s boat, at a dock off Catalina, squinting into the sun; Skye barefoot on the hood of the Saab with the top down, laughing at whoever has the camera.

Gina leaves the boat up. Rain ticks on the window over the sink, and Theo’s French pot has the gravy going on the back burner, and the Costigans and a Vance lean in around a fourteen-inch monitor on the kitchen table at a girl on a boat. In the picture her hair is wet and she has a can of Diet Coke in one hand and she’s laughing at somebody off the edge of the frame, and Jack knows that laugh; he has been the one off the edge of the frame. He keeps that off his face as well as he can. It isn’t very well.
The RAZR stays in Jack’s pocket, shut, with his hand on it.
“She’s in her underwear,” Ma says.
“It’s a *bathing suit*, Ma.”
“On a *boat*.”
Frank looks at the screen with his coffee halfway to his mouth, and doesn’t get it the rest of the way.
“Huh,” he says.
Nonna has her rosary out of her pocket. She says something low in Calabrese at the hood of the Saab, and then something lower.
“She says somebody get that girl a sweater,” Gina reports.
“And the other thing?”
“No.”
“Gina.”

“I will *never* say it.” Gina’s ears are red and she is having the best morning of her life. “Three seasons. She’s in every episode. The one who drowns in season two isn’t her. It’s really sad.” And low, to Jack, under the fan page: “I didn’t tell. I *gave you a present*.”
Rosie is kneeling up on a chair with her chin on the table and the blue crab under her arm. “She’s pretty.” She thinks about it. “Can I see the boat again?”
“No,” says Ma.
“There’s a promo,” Gina says. “For season three. She’s in a *pool*.”
“*No*,” says Ma.
Nonna lifts her chin off the beads and looks at Jack, very clear. “*E la suora?*”
Ma pulls her chair in closer to the table, and pushes it back out again. “What happened to the Saints girl?” she says. “She sent you a *book*.”
“The one he went out to the garage for,” Frank says.

Theo is at the counter with his coffee, in the hat and the scarf, the only one in the kitchen besides Jack who has ever met Skye Callender. “She’s very talented, Mrs. Costigan.” He drinks some coffee. “Lena called from a levee. It was on fire.”
“This one goes to school with you?” Ma says.
“Starting January.”
Ma, to the coffee: “Starting January.”

She gets up, and takes her cup to the sink, and runs the water with her back to all of them. Out the window over the sink the rain is coming down on the garage roof and the Madonna and the Kovacs’ fence, and the snow is going gray in the yard.
“Is she *Catholic*, at least?”

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it twenty-seven days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs.

response: “That’s not what I asked.” Ma turns the water up.
Ma turns around from the sink with the water still running. Theo sets his cup down on the counter and has to leave the room.

choices.text: “She’s trying to understand it, Ma. She asks me what it’s like.”
response: Ma turns the tap off and dries her hands on the towel over her shoulder. “Asking’s something.”
From her chair in the doorway Nonna says, “*Chiedere non è credere.*”

body: At a quarter past two the phone rings on the kitchen wall by the pantry, its long cord hanging down in loops to the linoleum, and Ma is there before the second ring with a dish towel in her other hand. The little set at the end of the counter has the news on low. A woman’s recorded voice comes out of the receiver loud enough for the table: *This is a collect call from* — and Danny, fast, saying his own name into the space they give him — *an inmate at an Ohio correctional institution. This call may be monitored and recorded.* Ma presses the button before the woman is finished.
“Merry Christmas, baby.”

She takes him into the pantry with the cord pinched under the door and is in there a minute with the canned tomatoes. When she comes out she holds the receiver down to Nonna’s chair in the doorway, and Nonna takes it in her left hand and listens with her eyes shut.
“Danny.” Then: “*Viene?*”
Ma takes it back from her gently and hands it on to Frank, who stands with the receiver against his ear and his other hand in his pocket and gives his son two sentences.
“Browns ran for two-eighty-six. Here’s your sister.”

Gina has been waiting. She takes the phone into the corner by the refrigerator, as far as the cord goes, and turns her back on the kitchen. It doesn’t help. “Danny. *Danny.* You don’t even know. She was on a *boat*. A boat with a *bathroom* on it. And then she’s barefoot on a *car* —”
“On a boat,” Ma says, at the stove.
“A *different* picture, Ma. Danny, there’s a fan page. Somebody in *Brazil* —” And out of the receiver, from across the kitchen, small and clear and helpless, comes Danny’s laugh.

Rosie gets the phone next, for about ten seconds, and spends them on the crab: it’s blue, it has a Latin name, the Latin name means *beautiful swimmer*, Theo said, Theo is here, Theo ate an eel. Danny is still laughing when Rosie hands the phone to Jack. Danny tries twice to say something and can’t get through it. The third time he makes it.
“You said she does *plays*.”
Gina wheels around by the refrigerator. “He *told* you?”
“He told me she *reads*, G,” Danny says, loud enough to carry, and keeps the rest. At the stove, with the wooden spoon stopped in the gravy, Ma looks at Jack, and then goes back to stirring.
“What’d you tell her, Professor?” Danny says. “You’re a doctor?”
“I told her about you.”
“Then she’s got guts,” Danny says. “Put the rich one on.”
Theo takes the phone in the orange hat. Danny’s voice comes out of it, tinny. “You came back.”
“Your father said I didn’t have to call first.”
“He said that?” Behind him, a room full of men and somebody’s name on a loudspeaker. “He never said that to nobody.”
Theo looks at the receiver in his hand. Then he gives it back to Jack fast, cord and all, and goes to see about the Tupperware.
There’s a tone on the line: a minute left. Danny comes back on lower, close to the mouthpiece, so whatever he means by it stays on Jack’s end.
“Tell the TV girl I said she can do better. And tell the veil girl —”
A click, and the dial tone.

Jack stands by the pantry with it humming in his ear. Gina is still holding her hand out for another turn. Nobody in the kitchen says anything, and after a minute Ma takes the receiver out of his hand and hangs it up on the wall.

At half past three the news on the little set changes its voice. A Northwest flight from Amsterdam, coming down into Detroit before noon: a passenger, something he had in his lap, a pop and then a fire, and the people around him on top of him before it could catch. They don’t have a name yet. They show a plane parked by itself, far out on the concrete.
“On *Christmas*,” Frank says.
Ma turns around from the stove. “You’re flying *tonight*?”
“They’ll be very thorough,” Theo says.

At half past four he comes down the stairs in the camel coat with the garment bag over his shoulder, in the Browns hat and the Browns scarf, without the parka. Jack carried his other bag down for him and saw it on the way, folded square at the foot of Danny’s bed. Ma has a Giant Eagle bag of Tupperware waiting by the side door, every lid labeled in her capitals: BACCALÀ. COOKIES. MORE COOKIES. FOR YOUR MOTHER. Rosie gives him a drawing of the crab. Gina films all of it on the Flip.

Nonna is in her chair in the front window with the cashmere over her knees and her hand on it. Theo bends down to her. She says something to him in Calabrese that Gina doesn’t translate, and pats his face, and he tucks the cashmere in along her side where it has come loose, and straightens up, and leaves it there.

body.text: At the side door he stops with his hand on the frame, and says it lower, under the noise of Ma looking for a bigger bag. “Be careful, Costigan.” “Of what?” “*All* of it.”

body: “Come back on the ninth,” Theo says, out on the step, with the rain coming off the gutter behind him. “Laney has a *schedule*.”
Jack laughs. “Of course she does.”
Frank has the Silverado running in the driveway with the wipers going. He leans across and shoves the passenger door open, and before Theo can get in he says it through the rain: “You come back.”
“I’ll call first, sir.”
“Don’t,” Frank says, and Theo gets in.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. I said it out loud: I’m in love with Lena. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Danny asked for him on the phone. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Three in the morning on Christmas, in Danny’s bed, I told him she’d told me. He wasn’t surprised.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.”

body: The tree is the only light on in the front room. Ma left the Christmas disc going for Nonna when she went up, low, and it has come around by now to the last track. The rain has eased to a drip off the porch roof, and the street outside is black and wet to the end of the block, the Santa two doors up face-down in the slush where the snow used to be. The house is asleep over his head. Gina’s light went off under her door at eleven. Upstairs, the parka is still folded on Danny’s bed, and Danny’s bed is made. On the mantel the eighth hook is empty; Theo took the stocking with him, glitter and all.

Nonna is awake in her chair by the window with Theo’s cashmere over her knees and the rosary moving in her good hand, a bead at a time, slower than the song. On the coffee table, under the markers in their open tin, is the drawing Rosie made after supper and left out for him: a girl in a navy blazer with yellow hair, and Jack beside her, very tall, and at their feet, bigger than either of them, a blue crab.
Jack sits down on the end of the couch in his socks, with the rain from the driveway still in his hair. He has had the phone in his hand since the truck. At two minutes to midnight it goes.

body.text: merry christmas from a hotel. my mother got a suite so nobody would have to cook. room service has a tree. its very small and very sad and i love it
cassidy says goodnight to your grandmother

body: He’s grinning at it in the dark. He can picture it: a hotel suite in Los Angeles, a tree no bigger than a lamp on the room-service cart, Skye in a hotel robe cross-legged on a bed the size of the Costigans’ kitchen, watching the clock on the cable box come around to nine. He can hear her doing Cassidy’s voice for the tree.

When he looks up, Nonna is watching him. She isn’t looking at his face. She’s looking at the phone, lit in his hand, with her head a little on one side, the way she looks at a pot she wasn’t told about.
“*Due ragazze*,” she says.
Then her eyes come up to his, and she is entirely here.
“*Quale ti fa pregare?*”
His Italian is church-and-kitchen. Out of all of it he has one word for certain, *pregare*. He knows that one.

He doesn’t answer her. After a while Nonna looks down again, and moves a bead along, and her lips start up where they left off. On the disc the song comes to its end, low, and stops. The tree lights stand in the wet window. Nonna’s beads click, and click again.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees.

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab.
